title: Japanese Daruma Doll
facts: This is a Daruma doll, a traditional Japanese good luck charm shaped like a round, hollow, weighted figure that always rolls back upright when you knock it over.
The doll is modeled after Bodhidharma, the monk who founded Zen Buddhism, who is said to have meditated facing a cave wall for nine years without moving, which is why the doll has no arms or legs.
Because it always returns to standing, the Daruma symbolizes perseverance and resilience, captured in the Japanese proverb nana korobi ya oki, meaning fall down seven times, get up eight.
Daruma dolls are traditionally papier mache and painted bright red, a color believed to ward off illness and misfortune, though today they come in many colors, each tied to a different kind of wish.
The doll is sold with two blank white eyes. When you set a goal or make a wish, you paint in one eye yourself, then paint the second eye only once that goal is achieved.
This eye-painting custom is called kaigan, meaning eye opening, and it turns the doll into a personal motivator that sits on your desk or shelf reminding you of your unfinished goal.

Daruma dolls are especially popular around New Year, when many Japanese people buy a fresh one, set a goal for the coming year, and burn last year's doll in a shrine ritual regardless of whether both eyes got painted.
The city of Takasaki in Gunma Prefecture is Japan's biggest producer of Daruma dolls, and its Shorinzan Daruma-ji temple holds a huge Daruma market every January that draws large crowds.
Daruma dolls are also popular in politics and business in Japan, where politicians and company presidents publicly paint in the first eye at the start of an election campaign or a big project.
The word Daruma is the Japanese phonetic abbreviation for "Bodhidharma," the Sanskrit name of the Indian monk who founded Zen Buddhism.

Daruma dolls trace back to a Japanese toy tradition called okiagari-koboshi, a weighted, bottom-heavy "get-up little monk" toy that always rights itself, which is where the doll's tumbling, self-righting shape comes from.
The design is closely associated with Shorinzan Daruma-ji, the temple in Takasaki, where monks are credited with popularizing the painted, wishing version of the doll that's common today.

In Japanese sports and business culture, teams, companies, and even political campaign offices buy an oversized Daruma and paint in one eye together as a public show of shared determination before a big challenge.

The bushy eyebrows and mustache painted on a Daruma's face are often stylized to look like a crane, and the beard around the chin like a tortoise shell, since both animals are traditional Japanese symbols of long life.
According to legend, Bodhidharma is also linked to the origins of Shaolin martial arts training in China, although historians debate how much of that story is later legend versus historical fact.
Daruma dolls range enormously in size, from palm-sized versions sold as souvenirs to towering festival dolls over a meter tall displayed at temple markets.

The seven-falls-eight-rises spirit behind the Daruma reflects a broader Japanese value called ganbaru, roughly "doing one's best and not giving up," which shows up throughout Japanese culture beyond just this doll.

Burning a doll at a shrine, called Daruma kuyo, is meant to thank it for its year of service rather than punish it for an unfinished goal, which is why people return old Daruma even if the second eye was never painted.

While red is the traditional color for general good luck, later variations use specific colors for specific wishes: gold for wealth, pink for love or relationships, and green for health, among others.
